name: Chisel
text: Adopt a **4-hour triage by Legal for obvious red flags**, then **auto-escalate every contract with non-standard language to a 24-hour human review by Legal**. This forces Legal to focus on the 20% of cases that actually hide real risks, cutting noise by 80%. The trade-off is accepting a small uptick in false positives—burying some standard deals in extra review—but it guarantees no high-risk clause slips through unchecked.

name: Sift
text: Custom terms are the highest-risk deals—so auto-escalating *all* non-standard language to Legal is the only safe play. The classifier’s blind spot on proprietary terms is a real gap; settle it by running the classifier *first*, then forcing a 24-hour Legal review on every flagged non-standard contract. That’s the trade-off: 100% coverage now, not 90%.

name: Scope
text: Adopt a **4-hour triage by Legal for obvious red flags**, then **auto-escalate only contracts flagged by a pre-trained classifier trained on public vendor contracts** to a **24-hour human review by Legal**. This balances speed and accuracy—catching 90% of high-risk clauses while cutting noise by 60%, without drowning Legal in 50-page reviews. The trade-off is accepting missed risks in custom or proprietary terms, but those are rare and can be handled case-by-case.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The classifier’s blind spot on custom terms isn’t a flaw—it’s the *real risk*. Auto-escalating *all* non-standard language to Legal for 24-hour review solves that by forcing human eyes on the highest-risk deals. Settle it with a pilot: run the classifier for two weeks, then compare its missed risks against Legal’s manual reviews—if the classifier misses more than 10% of high-severity clauses, scrap it.

name: Reel
text: Adopt a **pre-trained classifier trained on public vendor contracts** to auto-flag hidden clauses or third-party triggers within the 4-hour triage window. This shifts the burden from Legal’s domain expertise to a repeatable, scalable system, cutting false positives by 60% while catching 90% of high-risk cases. The trade-off is accepting missed risks in custom or proprietary terms—those will still require manual review, but the classifier handles the bulk of low-risk, high-volume cases first.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The classifier’s blind spot on custom terms isn’t a flaw—it’s the *real risk*. Auto-escalating *all* non-standard language to Legal for a 24-hour review creates a bottleneck that delays deals and burns Legal’s capacity on low-value noise. Instead, enforce the 4-hour triage for obvious red flags, then auto-escalate *only* contracts with third-party triggers or clauses matching known high-risk patterns—settle this by running a 30-day pilot with Legal tracking false negatives and false positives.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt a **4-hour triage by Legal for obvious red flags**, then **auto-escalate every contract with non-standard language to a 24-hour human review by Legal**. This forces Legal to focus on the 20% of cases that actually hide real risks, cutting noise by 80%. The trade-off is accepting a small uptick in false positives—some standard contracts will get reviewed unnecessarily—but it ensures no high-risk clause slips through.

name: Sift
text: The real risk in auto-escalating *all* non-standard language is that Legal will drown in false positives—custom terms aren’t always high-risk, just different. Instead, enforce the 4-hour triage for obvious red flags, then auto-escalate only contracts where the classifier flags *both* non-standard language *and* a domain-specific risk pattern (e.g., indemnity clauses in SaaS deals). Settle it by testing the classifier on 50 live custom contracts and measuring how many high-risk items it misses.
